analysis.one_liner: Bars airlines from charging fees that exceed their actual costs for changes, baggage, and seat selection.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have let the Transportation Department crack down on unreasonably high airline fees, never received a vote in the Senate before the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required the Department of Transportation to write rules forbidding airlines from charging passengers fees for changing or canceling tickets, checking bags, or picking seats unless those fees are reasonable and match the airline's actual costs. It would also have required the rules to guarantee that parents can sit next to their children age 13 or younger at no extra charge. The bill was introduced in February 2023, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, and never received any further action before the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers, especially families who face charges to sit together, budget travelers hit by checked-bag and seat-selection fees, and passengers whose plans change and face cancellation charges that far exceed the airline's actual cost of rebooking a seat.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Airline passengers and families flying with children

how_it_helps.text: The bill directs the Department of Transportation to write regulations within 270 days prohibiting air carriers from imposing fees for flight changes or cancellations, checked or carry-on baggage, and seat selection that are unreasonable or disproportional to the costs the airline actually incurs [S2] [S3].

In judging change and cancellation fees, the Secretary must weigh what the airline actually gains: its ability to resell the seat, the fare a new passenger would likely pay, the low electronic processing cost of a change, and related labor costs [S3].

For seat-selection fees, the bill requires the standards to ensure that passengers traveling with children age 13 or younger can be seated with those children at no additional charge to the family or to any other passenger on the flight [S3].

The Department must update the fee standards at least every three years, and the rules apply to all carriers holding an air carrier certificate, including foreign, interstate, and intrastate passenger flights [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, whose fee revenue (baggage fees, seat selection, change and cancellation charges) would be capped at roughly their actual costs. Passengers might also see some of that cost shifted back into base fares, since fees currently allow airlines to advertise lower headline ticket prices.

drawbacks.text: Cost-based fee caps could push airlines to fold some of that revenue back into base fares, so some travelers would pay more for the ticket itself even if fees shrink; airlines argue that unbundling fees lets occasional flyers who travel light pay less overall [S3].

The bill works entirely through Department of Transportation rulemaking, so its real-world effect would depend on how strictly the Secretary writes and enforces the 'reasonable and proportional' standards, which is a judgment call rather than a hard price cap [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a widespread, concrete cost to travelers: airlines collect billions of dollars a year in fees that often far exceed the cost of the service, and families are routinely charged extra just to sit with their own children. The main cost is that some of that revenue could shift back into base fares, and the standard leaves room for regulator judgment. On balance, the consumer protections are straightforward and the bill was modest in design, leaving the main question why it was never allowed a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in the Senate in February 2023 and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which never took it up, and it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the FAIR Fees Act in the Senate on February 1, 2023, joined by seven cosponsors, all Democrats or independents aligned with Democrats [S1] [S3] [S4].
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day [S5].
The full action history shows no further action: no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote, and no House counterpart action is recorded before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airlines are better off because the bill died: they keep charging baggage, seat-selection, and change fees unbound by any cost test, and families keep paying to sit with their children.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Airlines, which kept charging unregulated fees

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.role: U.S. Senator from Massachusetts; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAIR Fees Act of 2023 in the Senate.

for.name: Sens. Blumenthal, Brown, Sanders, Warren, Whitehouse, and Wyden
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it eight Senate supporters in total (including one independent).

against.name: Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill; the record shows no committee action after referral, so it never reached the Senate floor.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: No Republican cosponsored the bill, and with only Democratic support it lacked the 60 votes typically needed to advance to a floor vote.

sides.party_line_note: All eight supporters were Democrats or one independent aligned with Democrats; no Republican cosponsored, and the bill died in a committee chaired by a Democrat without ever reaching a vote.

industries.note: The bill would have capped the fees airlines charge for bagging luggage, choosing seats, and changing or canceling tickets at their actual cost, directly cutting into billions in ancillary fee revenue. Airlines' interest in keeping these fees high runs against travelers', since fees often far exceed the cost of the service and families pay extra to sit together.
